title: My Brother Threatened to Foreclose on My House, Not Knowing Who Owned It

author: admin

blocks.text: At my mother's 70th birthday dinner in Austin, my brother Wade raised his glass and said, "Kelly finally decided to pay the $96,800 she owes me for renovating her house."

There were fourteen people sitting around the long table in the private back room of the steakhouse. My aunts were there. My cousins were there. My husband, Ben, was sitting right next to me with his hand on my knee.
Our signed estimate was $78,000. I had already paid $72,000.
Wade didn't wait for me to answer. He reached inside his suit jacket, pulled out a folded piece of paper, and slid it across the white tablecloth toward my plate.
"I filed the lien Friday," he said, loud enough for the far end of the table to hear.
I picked up the paper. My hands were shaking a little, mostly from embarrassment.
It was a stamped Travis County mechanic's lien affidavit. Right there in black ink, Wade had listed $96,800 as the unpaid balance on my house on Briarwood Lane.
Ben leaned over and read it twice. His jaw tightened. "I never signed any construction contract with you, Wade."
Wade smiled like he had been waiting all night for Ben to say that. "Doesn't matter. Kelly did."
Around the table, nobody was eating anymore. My aunt Ruth stared down at her water glass. My cousin Mark suddenly got very interested in his napkin.
Then my mother leaned in close to my shoulder and whispered, "Please just pay your brother before he forecloses."
I looked at her. For seventy years, my mother had treated Wade like the golden boy who could never catch a break, and me like the sensible daughter who was always supposed to clean up his messes.

When his contracting business hit a slow patch last fall, I had hired him to redo our kitchen and back deck specifically to help him out. I could have hired two other crews for less, and Ben had warned me not to mix family and money. I didn't listen.
Wade leaned toward me across the corner of the table, lowering his voice just enough so only Ben, Mom, and I could hear him clearly.
"Monday, I start the process," he said. "You got forty-eight hours to wire the rest, Kelly. Or I take the house."
I looked at the stamped county seal at the bottom of the page. Then I looked at Wade's smug face.
He thought he had me cornered in front of the whole family. He thought I would panic and write a check just to keep the peace, the way I always had.
What Wade didn't know was that he had just filed a fraudulent lien against the wrong house.
Ben and I didn't stay for cake. I kissed my mother on the cheek, told her happy birthday, and walked out to our car with the lien paper folded in my purse.
In the parking lot, Ben unlocked the doors and looked at me over the roof of the SUV. "Tell me you didn't sign a change order for eighteen thousand dollars."

"I didn't," I said. "Not one. Every single tile, cabinet, and board we picked was inside that $78,000 estimate. And I have the bank receipts for the $72,000 I already sent him. The last $6,000 was supposed to be paid when he finished the back steps, which he still hasn't touched."
Ben got in the driver's seat and started the engine. "Then where did $96,800 come from?"
I went straight into my home office, turned on the desk lamp, and pulled the thick blue folder labeled Briarwood Renovation out of the bottom filing drawer.

Inside were the original signed estimate from October, every text message I had printed out when Wade started asking for early draws, and four wire transfer confirmations from our credit union totaling $72,000.
I spread them out on my desk next to Wade's county lien.

I read every line of the lien carefully. Toward the bottom, under the legal description of the property, Wade had typed in our street address: 412 Briarwood Lane, Austin, Texas. Under owner of record, he had typed my name: Kelly Ann Mercer.
I stared at that line for a full ten seconds.
Then I reached into the back of the drawer and pulled out a thinner manila folder.
On the tab, in Ben's neat handwriting, it read: Mercer Family Trust, Recorded 2019.

Five years earlier, right after Ben retired from his engineering firm and we paid off our mortgage, our estate attorney had advised us to transfer the deed of 412 Briarwood Lane into an irrevocable family trust for our two daughters. Neither Ben nor I owned the house in our individual names anymore. We were trustees, not personal owners, and under Texas property law, a contractor couldn't enforce a mechanic's lien against trust property unless the trust itself was named and both trustees signed the contract.
Ben had never signed anything. And my personal name wasn't even on the deed.
Wade hadn't bothered to run a basic title search before walking into the county clerk's office.
He had just assumed the house was in my name because I was the one who always paid the bills.
I picked up my phone and pulled up Wade's contact info, ready to text him and tell him his lien was worthless.
If I told him tonight, he would just fix the paperwork, or try to pressure me another way. More importantly, I still didn't know why my brother had suddenly invented a $96,800 debt out of thin air.
I set my phone down on the desk and opened my laptop instead.
If Wade wanted to play games with county records, I was going to look at every public record with his name on it before Monday morning.
Saturday morning, Ben made coffee while I sat at the kitchen island with my laptop and a yellow legal pad.
"Before we call our lawyer on Monday, I want to know why he did this," I said, scrolling through the Travis County clerk's public database.
"Wade cuts corners, Ben. He's lazy about permits and he always asks for money early. He's never flat-out lied about twenty-four thousand dollars."
Ben set a mug next to my elbow. "People do stupid things when they're desperate. Check his business filings."
I typed in Wade's company name, Hill Country Custom Builds LLC.
The business registration popped up right away. It was active, though he had filed his annual report late twice. I clicked over to the civil court index and searched his name and the company name.
Nothing came up under his personal name. Under the LLC, there was one small claims judgment from two years ago for $3,400 to a lumber yard in Round Rock, marked satisfied.
"Check surrounding counties," Ben said, leaning over the counter. "Hays, Williamson, Bastrop. He works all over the corridor."
I opened three new browser tabs and ran the same search in Williamson County first.
Two records came up immediately. Both were filed within the last six weeks.
The first was a lawsuit filed by a wholesale cabinet supplier out of Georgetown. They were suing Hill Country Custom Builds LLC and Wade personally for $41,200 in unpaid invoices.
The second was a notice of default on a commercial equipment loan for $28,500.
I sat back in my chair. My stomach felt hollow.
Ben read the screen over my shoulder. "Look at the filing date on that cabinet lawsuit. October 14. That's three days before he came to you asking for the kitchen renovation job."

I looked back at my blue folder on the counter. On October 17, Wade had shown up at my front door with a box of kolaches and a sad story about how a big commercial client had delayed a project until spring.
He had asked if Ben and I still wanted to remodel our kitchen, promising he would give us a "sister discount" at $78,000.
I had felt sorry for him. I had moved money out of a certificate of deposit early, taking a small interest penalty, just so I could give him a $30,000 deposit the very next day.

And he hadn't used my money to buy my cabinets. He had used my $72,000 to pay off old debts and keep his creditors from seizing his truck, and now he didn't have enough cash left to finish my house or pay the suppliers who were suing him.
"Wait a minute," Ben said, pointing at the screen. "Look at the math. He's being sued for $41,200. You owe him $6,000 when he finishes the back steps. Why did he put $96,800 on your lien?"
I picked up my pen and subtracted $72,000 from $96,800 on the legal pad.

"He's not trying to collect $96,800 from me," I said slowly, staring at the numbers. "He knows I already paid $72,000. He wrote the lien for the whole inflated amount so it looks like a massive debt on paper. That way, he can force me to hand over the $24,800 difference right now just to get the lien removed before Monday."
